Cour supérieure

Référence : H.
c.

R.

[1998] RL 98

H.

demandeur
—
intimé

c.

R.

intimée
—
demanderesse

C.S.M. n°
500-04-006344-965

22
juillet
1997

Présente: La juge
Jeannine M. Rousseau

Résumé de la Revue légale

LÉGISLATION

—
Code civil
du Québec
, L.Q. 1991, c. 64: 32, 33, 34, 597, 599, 600, 601, 603,
604, 605, 611, 612.

Famille — Autorité parentale — Droit
de garde — Intérêt de l’enfant — Devoirs des parents

Personne — Enfant — Intérêt de l’enfant — Droit de garde

Le tribunal considère qu’il est de son devoir
de rappeler aux parents certains faits essentiels: 1) Leur enfant est une personne distincte et différente de chacun d’eux — l’un est d’origine israélite, l’autre
d’origine égyptienne —, mais lui,
il fut conçu, est né et élevé au Canada, sa citoyenneté à lui est donc
canadienne; 2) Même si les parents
sont de religion différente (juive et catholique), ils ont consenti à ce que
leur enfant soit et circoncis et baptisé; 3) En résumé, leur enfant n’est ni un petit juif anglophone appelé «M.J.»
ni un petit catholique francophone appelé «M...» et ils doivent tous les deux
cesser de l’identifier à chacun d’eux.

• Requête en garde d’enfant, accueillie.

Jugement

TEXTE INTÉGRAL

[
1
]

The Court is seized with applications concerning M.-J. H., born in July 1994; custody, access and
alimentary support.

The facts

[
2
]

The child’s parents, T.R. and A.H., fell into
parenthood unexpectedly; they were 22 and 23 years old; both were working in
restaurants, each was living at home with their parents.

[
3
]

In January 1994, Miss R. began studying part-time at
Concordia University and continued working as a waitress; Mr H. was working
full time.

[
4
]

They started living together in May or June 1994,
shortly before the birth of the child, in an apartment they rented in Dorval;
in June 1995, they moved into a house in L’Île-Bizard which they had chosen, and which Mr H.’s parents had then bought and
rented to them.

[
5
]

In January 1995, she went back to work as a waitress
three to five days a week; she also took one course per semester.

[
6
]

During the summer of 1995, Miss R.’s parents moved to
Israel with her younger brother; her father, an engineer, had lost his job with
Paramax, when a substantial helicopter contract had been cancelled; he had been
unable to secure other employment and decided to return to Israel; Miss R. and
the baby accompanied them and remained there for two weeks, with the approval
and consent of Mr. H.

[
7
]

In October 1995, Miss R.’s mother came for a visit, at
Miss R.’s request, and stayed with the young couple for two to three months;
Miss R. had come to the conclusion her relationship with Mr H. was
unsatisfactory and that she would be leaving him; she had asked her mother to
come to help her through this difficult period.

[
8
]

Her mother left however in December 1995 without Miss
R. having separated from Mr H.; during these three months, Mr H. left for work
early and came home late; he knew why Miss R.’s mother was there,
i.e.
to help her
daughter leave him, and felt uncomfortable; thus, he made himself scarce.

[
9
]

The separation occurred in February 1996, when Miss R.
moved out with the child; she rented an apartment in Saint-Laurent, near Mr
H.’s place of employment and the child’s day-care; Miss R. and Mr H. had agreed
the baby would stay with her but could see Mr H. or the paternal grand-parents
whenever they wanted.

[
10
]

From February to May 1996, a
modus vivendi

developed: Miss R. was working and studying; Mr H. was working.

[
11
]

Miss R. brought the child to the day-care in the
morning and picked him up in the evening: sometimes the paternal grand-parents
would pick him up.

[
12
]

Mr H. remained in the L’Île-Bizard
house.

[
13
]

In May 1996, Miss R. left written instructions at the
day-care that no one was to pick up the child without her being informed:

May 27, 96

“Starting from May 29th, 1996 only
M.J’s mother (T.R.) will be taking M.-J. from the day-care — If anyone else
attempts to take him from the daycare, I must be notified immediately.

[Phone]
Dom.

[Phone]
tr.

Thank
you,

T.R.

T.R.”

(Exhibit R-2)

[
14
]

She had felt this to be necessary because she had come
to the conclusion the paternal grand-mother was acting as if she wanted to take
over the mother’s role and was not ready to follow the mother’s requests or
instructions.

[
15
]

The other factor which made her give these instructions
to the daycare was the pressure put on her by the paternal grand-father to sign
a proposed agreement; he told her that if she did not sign by the Monday, they
would take the child away; Miss R. knew Mr H. would not take the baby away, but
she felt scared; so she wrote the note so as to be advised if anyone picked the
baby up.

[
16
]

Unfortunately, she did not tell Mr H. about these
instructions, nor explain why.

[
17
]

Thus, when the paternal grand-mother arrived at the
day-care the next day to bring the child, who had spent the night at her house,
she was informed of these instructions; seeing that no mention was made of even
the father being entitled to pick up the child without the mother being
informed, she did not leave him there; she went, with the child, to her son’s
home on L’Île-Bizard and informed
him of these instructions.

[
18
]

The events of the next days were a horror and appear in
the record.

[
19
]

The parties ended up in Court on June 6, 1996, when
Miss R. was granted interim custody, with defined access for Mr H.

[
20
]

Another crisis occurred in July 1996, when Miss R.
suddenly left with the child for Israel, without telling Mr H.; this is
discussed more fully later.

[
21
]

She called him upon her arrival and there were
telephone conversations back and forth during her stay there; arrangements were
negotiated by the parties’ lawyers for access to resume upon her return; they
were to meet at the paediatrician’s office, where the child had an appointment
for a regular visit, on August 1st, 1996.

[
22
]

The meeting went very badly; they fought in the parking
lot and Mr H. drove off in a fury.

[
23
]

Mr H. took a two-week vacation in August 1996; he went
to the United States East Coast with a group of friends; he did not bring the
child; upon his return, he asked Miss R. for a two-week period with the child;
she refused.

[
24
]

Before the Court, she stated she saw no reason for it,
as he was going back to work; if he did not care enough to take holiday time
with his son, why should he spend time with him when he was working.

[
25
]

Before the Court, Mr H. stated he was planning to take
another two-week holiday to spend with the child; but as Miss R. refused the
two-week access period, he did not and worked instead.

[
26
]

The motions were scheduled for hearing at the end of
October, but got postponed to January 1997.

[
27
]

In September 1996, Miss R. increased her courses to
full time: she is studying administration at Concordia University previously,
she had been studying part-time.

[
28
]

In November 1996, the Rental Board allowed her to move
out of her Ville Saint-Laurent
apartment because of security and sanitary deficiencies.

[
29
]

She was unable to find another suitable apartment in
the Saint-Laurent area; she did find one however in the Notre-Dame-de-Grâce/Snowdon area and moved there in December; shortly thereafter, she
transferred the child to a new day-care centre, nearer her home; she had told
Mr H. she was planning to change day-care centre, he told her he did not want
her to, and the conversation ended there; she did it anyway.

[
30
]

At Christmas, she joined the H. family for the exchange
of presents at the paternal grand-mother’s residence.

[
31
]

The trial began on January 22, 1997; Mr H.’s father
died that evening; and the trial was postponed to May 8 and 9,1997.

The trial

The trial lasted three days; nine
witnesses were heard:

– Miss R.;

– Mr H.;

– Dr Patricia Green Mailberg, an independent witness to the August 1st
fight in the parking lot;

– E.C., a close friend of Miss R.;

– N.H., the paternal grand-mother;

– M.A., a close friend of Mr H.,
the fiancé of his sister and the
child’s godfather;

– N.D., the girl-friend of another
close friend of Mr H.;

– P.A., Mr H.’s employer, and the
girl-friend of Mr H. deceased father;

– Dr F.A., a professor of neurology and paediatrics at Montreal
Neurological Institute and the Montreal Children’s Hospital, a member of Miss
R. family — he and Miss R. father are second cousins.

The issues

[
32
]

The issues to be decided are custody and access;
alimentary support; and authorisation for Miss R. to visit her family in Israel
for a few weeks every summer with the child.

Custody

[
33
]

Miss R. requests full custody; she does not want joint
custody because she and the father cannot talk without fighting; she is of the
opinion he wants to control her and will not agree to anything.

[
34
]

Mr H. would have preferred joint custody; but under the
circumstances, as Miss R. does not agree, he is asking for full custody; if
Miss R. gets custody, he requests as much access as possible.

[
35
]

As mentioned above, Mr H. and Miss R. became parents
unexpectedly; they did not have much time to learn to become parents together;
and they have failed dismally in learning to be parents living apart: they
don’t even call the child by the same name: “M.” and “M.J.”!

[
36
]

There is distrust on both sides; there is no real
communication:

[
37
]

Miss R. states what she wants to do, Mr H. states he
does not agree; she does it anyway, he gets angry and feel frustrated.

[
38
]

Over and above these customary issues which come up
frequently in disputed custody cases, the intertwined issues of religion and
language are present, as well as that of race, though to a lesser degree:

– Miss R. was born in Israel; she
came to Canada with her parents and brother in 1982, when she was nine years
old; they lived in Calgary for some years; in 1987 the family moved to
Montreal; and, as related above, her parents and brother returned to Israel in
1995; she is a Canadian citizen and holds a Canadian passport; however she also
holds an Israeli passport, issued in Montreal in July 1996; an Israeli passport
was also issued for the child at the same time.

– Mr H. was born in Egypt; he was
18 years old when he came to Canada with his parents and sister in 1989; his
father died here in January 1997; his mother, his sister and her fiancé live in the Montreal area; Mr H. is a
Canadian citizen.

– Miss R. is Jewish; Mr H. is an
Orthodox Catholic; both are Canadian citizens.

– Miss R. speaks English and
Hebrew, as well as French to a certain extent; Mr H. speaks French; he also
speaks English, but the Court does not know to what extent; the Court presumes
he speaks Arabic, as Miss R. stated she has no objection if he wants to teach
the child Arabic.

When asked by the Court in which
language the couple talked to each other during their relationship, Mr H. said
a bit in both English and French.

– Since December 1996, the child
has been attending, against Mr H.’s wishes, a day-care centre run by
Garderie du Centre
communautaire
juif de Montréal
; Jewish
religious feasts and traditions are observed.

– There is thirty minutes a week of
instruction in the Hebrew language; some of the staff speak to the child in
French, some in English, and some in Hebrew.

Miss R. speaks to the child in
English as well as in Hebrew; she wants him to be able to communicate with her
relatives in Israel.

Mr H. speaks to him in French.

– Mr H. calls the child “M.”; it
was his own father’s name and, according to his family’s tradition, each
first-born son is named for his grand-father; thus, over the generations, the
H. men are called “A.” and “M.” sequentially; M., A., M., A., etc.

Miss R. is of the opinion “M.” or
“M.” is a common name; she would have preferred something more original; but
she had no choice as to “M.”; however she and Mr H. were able to agree on “J.”
as a second given name; it was the name of her own grandfather.

Thus the child’s given names are
“M.J.”; and Miss R. calls him “M.J.”; she feels it is distinctive and cute.

– Miss R. would have liked to have
the child bear her surname, as well as that of Mr H.

Mr H. did not agree; according to
Miss R.’s uncontradicted testimony, he felt it would be a handicap to have a
Jewish name — “R.” — which could lead to discrimination; Miss R. did not agree
it would be a handicap to have a Jewish name.

– The child was symbolically
brought into both religions; he was circumcised when he was eight days old;
Miss R.’s uncle flew in from Israel to attend; he was baptised in the Catholic
Church when he was one year old.

Mr H. agreed to the ritual circumcision but did not attend.

Miss R. agreed to and attended the
baptism; she and Mr H. together selected M.A. as godfather; her parents however
were not invited to attend the baptism party by the paternal grand-parents
because Mr H. felt they would not want to attend; had they been invited, she
stated, her mother would certainly have come, even though she had just moved to
Israel; she herself did not invite her parents as she felt it was not up to her
to do so.

Thus each side of the family got
its own ceremony.

– According to Miss R.’s
uncontradicted testimony, Mr H. is afraid that if the child is brought up as a
Jew, he will end up hating him, as Jew hate Arabs.

In Miss R.’s mind, her son is Jewish;
she states, however, that she has no objection to Mr H. celebrating Christian
feasts with him,
i.e.
Christmas and Easter.

– It must be noted that in both
families, there have been parents or grand-parents of the other faith; but
these were not cases of religious coexistence; there were conversions or
silence,
i.e.
the fact was hidden.

Miss R.’s mother was brought up as
a Christian; it was only when she was 16 years old that she found out her
father was Jewish; it had never been talked about; she investigated that aspect
of her heritage and decided that she wanted to live as a Jew.

Mr H.’s maternal grand-mother was
born a Jew; she converted to Christianity when she married.

[
39
]

Thus, neither Mr H. nor Miss R. have examples of
respectful accommodation or coexistence to rely upon; neither family provides
them with experiences to draw upon.

[
40
]

They are going to have to find their own way.

[
41
]

It is clear to the Court, however, that the conflicts
concerning the child are more cultural than religious, even though there is a
religious component:

– Neither parent is particularly
religious; there was no evidence of attendance at religious ceremonies during
their life together or since their separation.

– Miss R. pointed out that the child’s
day-care was not a religious school; the children are not made to pray; they
are introduced to the various Jewish feasts and the school’s calendar reflects
this; it also reflects Christmas to a certain extent,
i.e.
to the extent that Canadian society has made
Christmas into a secular holiday period for all; Miss R. stated that the
day-care represented to her a continuation of her family and that it was a
learning experience for her too.

– Mr H.’s concern is not that the
child, if brought up as a Jew, will dislike him because he is a Christian; Mr
H.’s fear of dislike by his son relates to the fact he is an Arab.

[
42
]

Miss R.’s lawyer submitted authorities concerning
custody and religion. They are interesting, but not particularly useful,
because we are not here faced with a purely religious question.

[
43
]

It is the Court’s duty to remind the parents of certain
basic facts:

1. Their child is a person
different and separate from each of them; they may be of a Middle Eastern
origin,
i.e.
Israeli and Egyptian, but the child is from Canada: he was
conceived, born and is being brought up in Canada; he may be entitled to other
citizenship as well, but his own is Canadian.

2. Even though each parent’s
religious affiliation is different: the mother is Jewish and the father is
Catholic, the child has been initiated into and recognised by both communities:
he was circumcised as well as baptised; and this was done to the knowledge and
with the consent of both parents.

3. In summary, their child is
neither a little Jewish English-speaking boy called “M.J.”, nor a little
Catholic French-speaking boy called “M.”, and both parents are going to have to
stop seeing him as a prolongation of one or of the other.

4. The child is entitled to become
knowledgeable of both sets of religious tenets; a healthy dose of ecumenism is
called for, as each parent is to be respectful of their child’s duality, they
are both going to have to become more knowledgeable of the other parent’s
religious organisation; knowledge will do away with prejudices and make each
parent more comfortable with the other’s religious and cultural background;
thus Mr H. would no longer, rightly
or wrongly, feel uneasy and uncomfortable at the child’s present day-care.

5. Moreover, it would be in the child’s
interest to spend some substantial part of his pre-school years in a secular
day-care where both parents will feel as welcome the one as the other; this
would certainly defuse the tension between them and allow them to act on the
other issues.

6. Mr H. is going to have to stop
being scared or panicky every time a new issue occurs; and Miss R. is going to
have to stop considering the child as mostly hers and doling out access when
she feels it appropriate, as she did in August 1996: it is not up to one parent
to tell the other how to take care of the child nor how to spend his or her
time with the child; they both love the child; there is no reason not to trust
this love.

[
44
]

Let us go back to the basics of the
Civil Code of
Quebec
: the child, his interests, his rights; the parents and their duties:

32.
Tout enfant a droit à la protection, à la sécurité et à l’attention
que ses parents ou les personnes qui en tiennent lieu peuvent lui donner.

32.
Every child has a right
to the protection, security and attention that his parents or the persons
acting in their stead are able to give to him.

33.
Les décisions concernant l’enfant doivent
être prises dans son intérêt et dans le respect de ses droits

33.
Every decision concerning a child shall be taken in light of the
child’s interests and the respect of his rights.

Sont
pris en considération, outre les besoins moraux, intellectuels, affectifs et
physiques de l’enfant, son âge, sa santé, son caractère, son milieu familial
et les autres aspects de sa situation.

Consideration
is given, in addition to the moral, intellectual, emotional and material
needs of the child, to the child’s age, health, personality and family
environment and to the other aspects of his situation.

34.
Le tribunal doit, chaque fois qu’il est
saisi d’une demande mettant en jeu l’intérêt d’un enfant, lui donner la
possibilité d’être entendu si son âge et son discernement le permettent.

34.
The court shall, in every application brought before it affecting
the interest of a child, give the child an opportunity to be heard if his age
and power of discernment permit it.

597.
L’enfant à tout âge, doit respect à ses père
et mère.

597.
Every child, regardless of age, owes respect to his father and
mother.

599.
Les père et mère ont, à l’égard de leur
enfant, le droit et le devoir de garde, de surveillance et d’éducation.

599.
The father and mother have the rights and duties of custody,
supervision and education of their children.

Ils
doivent nourrir et entretenir leur enfant.

They
shall maintain their children.

600.
Les père et mère exercent ensemble
l’autorité parentale.

600.
The father and mother exercise parental authority together.

Si l’un
d’eux décède, est déchu de l’autorité parentale ou n’est pas en mesure de
manifester sa volonté, l’autorité est exercée par l’autre.

If
either parent dies, is deprived of parental authority or is unable to express
his or her will, parental authority is exercised by the other parent.

601.
Le titulaire de l’autorité parentale peut
déléguer la garde, la surveillance ou l’éducation de l’enfant.

601.
The person having parental authority may delegate the custody,
supervision or education of the child.

603.
À l’égard des tiers de bonne foi, le père ou
la mère qui accomplit seul un acte d’autorité à l’égard de l’enfant est
présumé agir avec l’accord de l’autre.

603.
Where the father or the mother performs alone any act of
authority concerning their child, he or she is, with regard to third persons
in good faith, presumed to be acting with the consent of the other parent.

604.
En cas de difficultés relatives à l’exercice
de l’autorité parentale, le titulaire de l’autorité parentale peut saisir le
tribunal qui statuera dans l’intérêt de l’enfant après avoir favorisé la
conciliation des parties.

604.
In the case of difficulties relating to the exercise of parental
authority, the person having parental authority may refer the matter to the
court, which will decide in the interst of the child after fostering the
conciliation of the parties.

605.
Que la garde de l’enfant ait été confiée à
l’un des parents ou à une tierce personne, quelles qu’en soient les raisons,
les père et mère conservent le droit de surveiller son entretien et son
éducation et sont tenus d’y contribuer à proportion de leurs facultés.

605.
Whether custody is entrusted to one of the parents or to a third
person, and whatever the reasons may be, the father and mother retain the
right to supervise the maintenance and education of the children, and are
bound to contribute thereto in proportion to their means.

611.
Les père et mère ne peuvent sans motifs
graves faire obstacle aux relations personnelles de l’enfant avec ses
grands-parents.

611.
In no case may the father or mother, without a grave reason,
interfere with personal relations between the child and his grandparents.

À défaut
d’accord entre les parties, les modalités de ces relations sont réglées par
le tribunal.

Failing
agreement between the parties, the terms and conditions of these relations
are decided by the court.

612.
Les décisions qui concernent les enfants
peuvent être révisées à tout moment par le tribunal, si les circonstances le
justifient.

612.
Decisions concerning the children may be reviewed at any time by
the court, if warranted by circumstances.

[
45
]

To whom should custody of the child be entrusted, given
the child’s rights as set out above and the parents’ responsibilities as set
out above?

[
46
]

The Court comes to the conclusion, with certain
reservations however, that legal custody of the child should be entrusted to
the mother: she has shown that she can take care of the child’s physical,
emotional, moral and intellectual needs.

[
47
]

The Court’s reservations come from Miss R.’s clear
tendency to take the child over as her own, to appropriate the child to herself
exclusively:

– Her instructions to the child’s
day-care in May 1996 that no one was to be allowed to take the child without
her authorisation (see Exhibit R-2 above).

True, Miss R. explained why she
gave these instructions: she was under pressure to sign an agreement and she
felt her decisions, as the mother of the child, were not being given sufficient
respect by the paternal grand-mother; her reaction was understandable; she
wanted to affirm her authority as the mother of the child; however, she acted
impulsively, without thinking her course of action through; there was no
mention of the father; there was not even any notice to the father; basically
she did not take the father into consideration; the father’s reaction of fear
was predictable, which is not to say his subsequent actions and those of his
family were not exaggerated.

– In July 1996, very shortly after
the interim judgment of the Honourable Justice A.-M. Trahan, of June 6, 1996,
pursuant to the crisis brought about by Miss R.’s note (Exhibit R-2), Miss R.
left for Israel with the child, without prior notice to the father; because the
Canadian passports were not in her possession, Miss R. had to get Israeli
passports for herself and the child in Montreal; this took a few days; she
would have had time to talk to Mr H., albeit through their lawyers, but she
chose not to; she was concerned she would be prevented from leaving, so she
chose not to face the problem and basically ran away.

Her reason for this abrupt
departure was her mother’s state of health: Miss R. testified that when she
called to talk to her mother in Israel, as she did regularly, she was told by
her aunt that her mother could not come to the phone, that she was in bed, was
not getting up and refusing to talk to anyone; to Miss R., this was
incomprehensible; she was very close to her mother and for the latter to refuse
to talk to her daughter on the phone, something must be very wrong; this was
Miss R.’s conclusion; thus, she decided to leave for Israel and see for
herself.

The Court is far from sure Miss
R.’s version of the facts is true; if Mrs R. was really sick, could not Miss R.
have waited to get information through her father, who was in Montreal at the
time and with whom she flew to Israel? If Mrs R. was really sick, with some
identifiable illness, why was there no proof of it? There was no attempts even
to prove it: no medical certificate, no hospitalisation certificate, not even a
diagnosis, a name to the illness, a description of treatment, nothing.

This departure for Israel has all
the hallmarks of a possible flight home to her parents.

Be that as it may, Miss R. did
return, but again, as in May 1996, she acted impulsively, without due regard
for the father’s rights and responsibilities.

– In December 1996, when Miss R.
changed the child’s day-care from Ville Saint-Laurent to Snowdon, again, she disregarded the father’s wishes
and input and their child’s duality by choosing a day-care center clearly
oriented to her own origins.

Miss R. should reflect how she
would feel if the shoe were on the other foot and Mr H. had enrolled the child
in a clearly Arab and catholic day-care, where the various feasts of the
catholic calendar were celebrated, such as St. Catherine’s feast day, the
patron saint of musicians; Advent; the Feast of the Immaculate Conception;
Christmas; New Year’s Day (Circumcision of Christ); Epiphany; Lent; the Feast
of St. Joseph; Palm Sunday; Holy Thursday; Good Friday; Easter Sunday; the
Feast of the Ascension; the Feast of “Fête-Dieu”; the Feast of St. Anne, Christ’s “grandmother”; the Assumption; etc.

All kinds of pleasant and
interesting stories around these feasts, and others, can give rise to amusing
and informative activities for the children, in the same fashion as it is done
it the day-care which the child presently attends and where feasts from the
Jewish religious calendar are celebrated.

Mr H. stated he felt uncomfortable
when he went to pick up the child at the day-care center; he did not linger, he
did not talk to the “educateurs”; he
felt he was treated differently because he was of Arab origin.

The Court does not know if Mr H. is
super sensitive or not or whether he is imagining things; most probably, if he
himself were less reserved, he might elicit a warmer response.

But Miss R. should reflect on how
she might feel if, for example, the hypothetical day-care center described
above were run by members of a religious order,
e.g.
nuns; might she not
feel, rightly or wrongly, a bit insecure, shut out, unsure of herself and of
her welcome?

In summary, Miss R. needs to
develop some empathy.

– A final incident which
illustrates the fact Miss R. has a clear tendency to take over the child as her
own and to minimise the father’s involvement or importance, appears from
Exhibit R-5.

It is the registration form she
filled in for the day-care center the child presently attends: in the space
provided for the father’s name, address, phone number and occupation, nothing
is written; there is even a slash across the lines; the message is clear: there
is no father to take into consideration, to notify, to inform, etc.; the father
is unimportant or inexistant.

Miss R. explained she had not
filled in his name because she was the only person dealing with the day-care;
she countered this proof with the statement she had included his name on the
other part of the form; true, she had; but it appears under the heading
“Special Authorization (if applicable)” as that of a person entitled to visit
the child during day-care hours.

That is far from being the rightful
place for a father’s name to appear, as father; once again, Miss R. downgrades
him to the role of a minor player.

The Court also notes that Mr H.’s
home address and work and cellular phone numbers are written below, but in a
different handwriting.

[
48
]

In attempting, consciously or unconsciously, to
eliminate Mr H. and preventing him from playing a parent’s role in their son’s
life, Miss R. is being unfair to the child: he is entitled to know and love
both parents, and to draw from both families, both origins and both sources and
traditions.

[
49
]

In summary, the above actions by Miss R. and the
underlying principle,
i.e.
the unimportance of the father, are of concern to the Court and
explain its reservations in granting custody to Miss R. Should her approach not
change, more conflicts can be expected.

What about access?

It should be frequent and regular

– every second week-end, from
Thursday afternoon to Monday morning; the child is to be picked up at the
day-care center on Thursday and returned there Monday;

– every Tuesday evening until
Wednesday morning: the child is to be picked up at the day-care center on
Wednesday and returned there the next morning;

– on Father’s Day, it being
understood the child shall be with the mother on Mother’s Day;

– four weeks each summer,
i.e.
two consecutive
weeks twice;

– the first half of the Christmas
holidays;

– during the Easter Week-end; if
Passover and Easter coincide, the time shall be shared equally;

it being understood however that the
child shall be with his mother during the Rosh Hashanah – Yom Kippur period.

Yearly visit to Israel and other travels

[
50
]

Miss R. requests authorisation to visit her parents and
sibling in Israel for two weeks each summer. It is a reasonable request and
shall be granted.

[
51
]

Because of the yet unsettled relationship between Mr H.
and Miss R., in particular their difficulty to discuss and settle issues
concerning their child and their lack of trust the one in the other, it is in
the child’s interest to set certain parameters so as to defuse the issue of
travel outside the Greater Montreal area: if either parent plans to travel with
the child outside the territory of the Montreal Urban Community for seven days
or more, he or she is to advise the other parent of that fact at least a week
before and to provide the proposed itinerary, as well as names, addresses and
telephone numbers where he or she can be reached; in the case of such an
absence of more that fourteen days, there shall be a weekly telephone call
placed by the travelling parent so that the child may “communicate” with the
other parent and up to date information be provided by the travelling parent to
the parent remaining at home.

[
52
]

In case of any similar absence by a parent without the
child, a similar arrangement would be desirable, but the Court shall not make
an order to that effect, leaving it to the parties to comply on their own.

Conclusions

Grants custody of M.-J. H., born
July 13, 1994, to T.R., his mother;

Grants access between the child and
A.H., his father, as follows:

– every second week-end, from
Thursday afternoon to Monday morning; the child is to be picked up at the
day-care center on Thursday and returned there Monday;

– every Tuesday evening until
Wednesday morning; the child is to be picked up at the day-care center on
Wednesday and returned there the next morning;

– on Father’s Day, it being
understood the child shall be with the mother on Mother’s Day;

– four weeks each summer,
i.e.
two consecutive
weeks twice;

– the first half of the Christmas
holidays;

– during the Easter Week-end; if
Passover and Easter coincide, the time shall be shared equally;

– at any other time agreed upon by
the parties;

it being understood however that the
child shall be with his mother during the Rosh Hashanah – Yom Kippur period;

[

]

Orders both parties, if they are to travel with the
child, to respect the following conditions: if either parent plans to travel
with the child outside the territory of the Montreal Urban Community for seven

]

]
